> 企者不立，跨者不行；自見者不明，自是者不彰，自伐者無功，自矜者不長.

Chapter 23 said: what is over-driven cannot last. Chapter 24 pulls the camera in and shows what over-driving actually looks like.

Two movements, four consequences, one verdict.

The movements: 企 — standing on tiptoe. 跨 — striding, legs spread wide. Both are ways of getting taller or faster by leaving the ground.

The verdict: 餘食贅行. Leftover food, and a tumor.

## 企 and 跨

No metaphorical softening is needed here. These are body movements, and their failure is physical.

Stand on tiptoe and you are taller for a moment and cannot stand. Not "should not" — cannot. The position is unstable by construction.

Stride with the legs spread and you cover more ground per step and cannot walk. The gait is not sustainable, so it is not a gait.

Both movements are attempts to get the result without the structure. And both fail in exactly the way the structure would have prevented.

## Four 不

The four negations are the same four as chapter 22, and their position here is the point: chapter 22 said what happens when the self is not paraded; chapter 24 says what happens when it is.

- 自見者不明 — the one who displays himself is not clear.
- 自是者不彰 — the one who insists he is right is not evident.
- 自伐者無功 — the one who claims credit has no merit registered.
- 自矜者不長 — the one who exalts himself does not last.

These are not punishments. Each is the mechanism described from the failure side: display obstructs clarity, insistence obstructs being seen, credit-claiming obstructs the credit, self-inflation obstructs duration.

## 餘食贅行

Two images, one meaning, and neither is polite.

餘食 is leftover food — the meal that has already been eaten and is now sitting there, no longer nourishing, still occupying the table. 贅行 is a tumor, a growth: extra tissue that has no function and consumes the body's resources.

Both images say the same thing about the tiptoe and the stride: this is not a lesser version of the right action; it is matter that has attached itself to the action and is now feeding on it.

That is why the chapter is the least courteous in the book. It is not saying "you could do better." It is saying: this part of what you are doing is not doing anything, and it is growing.

## 物或惡之，故有道者不處

Things may dislike it — and therefore the one who has the way does not 處 there.

或 is doing real work in that sentence. Not "everything hates it," but "some things may." Laozi does not claim universal revulsion; he claims that the residue is detectable, that whatever is near it registers it.

處 is the key verb: not 為 (do), not 行 (go), but 處 — to dwell, to reside. The instruction is not "don't tiptoe"; it is "don't live there."

You will tiptoe sometimes. There are moments that require reaching above your height. The failure is when the reaching becomes the address.

## Why this chapter belongs after 23

二十三 says intensity is expensive and therefore short. 二十四 shows the bill: the extra motion has become mass, and the mass is what has to be carried.

Which is the practical form of 餘食贅行 — not a moral category but a weight. The person who has been tiptoeing for years is not taller. They are heavier.

## A test

Find one thing you do that requires holding yourself slightly above your actual position — a tone, a claim, a pace. Notice how much of your day goes into maintaining the height. That maintenance is the 贅.
